newsitem.title: AZERBAIJAN: Baku alarmed by Moscow arms supplies to Armenia.
newsitem.headline: Baku alarmed by Moscow arms supplies to Armenia.

text.p: Azerbaijan rang alarm bells on Friday about massive Russian arms supplies to its neighbour and foe Armenia, but Azeri leaders stressed that the affair should not harm relations between Baku and Moscow.

The chairman of the Azeri parliament, Murtuz Aleskerov, said Moscow's arms shipments to Armenia, which according to a senior Russian politician totalled $1 billion in 1993-1996, could destabilise the volatile Transcaucasus region.
"If these arms are not returned this could lead to a new large-scale war in the region," he said at parliamentary hearings.

Russian media reported last month that dozens of tanks and armoured personnel carriers had been flown to Armenia which is involved in a bitter territorial dispute with Azerbaijan over the enclave of Nagorno-Karabakh.
Tens of thousands of people were killed on both sides after the age-old conflict flared up again in the late 1980s before the two sides struck a truce in 1994.

Interfax news agency said on Friday that the head of defence committee in Russia's State Duma (lower house of parliament), Lev Rokhlin, told closed hearings earlier this week that actual supplies of Russian arms to Armenia had been much bigger.
Rokhlin has said that the shipments also included dozens of missile-launchers, hundreds of anti-aircraft rockets and a large amount of ammunition.
Rokhlin also said that the arms were handed over to the Armenians illegally, bypassing parliament.

Azeri President Haidar Aliev summoned top officials on Friday to discuss the incident. His press office said he had sent a message to Yeltsin urging the Kremlin leader to have the arms sent back to Russia.
The Azeri ambassador in Russia, Ramiz Rizayev, told a news conference in Moscow that the Kremlin had promised to investigate the incident.
"I believe that President (Boris) Yeltsin and Prime Minister (Viktor) Chernomyrdin knew nothing about this," Rizayev said.
He said that the Russian leaders had promised their cooperation in investigating the scandal.

"Even before the latest revelations we raised this issue with Moscow during the Commonwealth meeting," Rizvayev said in reference to last month's summit meeting of the 12 ex-Soviet republics which form the Commonwealth of Independent States.
"I was there at talks between Aliyev and Chernomyrdin," he said. "Chernomyrdin promised to investigate the whole thing and report by the next Commonwealth summit in the summer."

Rizayev said that the scandal over the arms shipments had erupted at a time when uneasy relations between Moscow and Baku had started improving following Yeltsin's replacement of his hawkish Defence Minister Pavel Grachev and pro-Western Foreign Minister Andrei Kozyrev last year.
Baku was satisfied with Russia's latest mediatory efforts in its talks with Armenia and Karabakh separatists, he said.
The Armenians had the upper hand in the fighting and still control a large swathe of Azerbaijan -- Karabakh and the territory surrounding it.

Rizayev also said that the new, "more realistic" stance taken by current Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov gave hope of sorting out another painful issue in bilateral relations -- a dispute about jurisdiction over the oil-rich Caspian Sea.
